overview: The ransomware.live Education sector dataset returned 1,296 named victims spanning 2016 through 20 July 2026. Volume by year shows the sector's escalation and persistence: 2016 (2), 2017 (1), 2018 (2), 2019 (4), 2020 (15), 2021 (74), 2022 (157), 2023 (307), 2024 (248), 2025 (328), and 158 already recorded in the first ~7 months of 2026. 2023 and 2025 are the peak full years; the 2024 dip did not hold, and 2026 is tracking broadly in line with recent years. Attribution is highly fragmented, with 135 distinct groups named. The top claimants across the full period are lockbit3 (114), qilin (73), incransom (72), vicesociety (63), rhysida (57), pysa (50), medusa (45), clop (44), ransomhub (43), and safepay (39); the top ten groups account for only 46.3% of postings, confirming a long tail of smaller and short-lived brands. Composition has shifted materially: restricting to 2025-2026, the leaders become qilin (65), incransom (47), safepay (29), interlock (25), thegentlemen (24), lockbit5 (19), fog (19), nova (18), shinyhunters (14), and rhysida (13) - i.e. LockBit-era dominance and the education-specialist Vice Society and PYSA brands have been displaced by Qilin, INC Ransom, Interlock and SafePay, alongside pure-extortion actors such as ShinyHunters. Geographically the sector is heavily US-weighted: of 947 records with a resolved country, the US accounts for 519 (54.8% of known-country victims, 78 countries represented in total). Other leading countries are GB (66), FR (31), CA (30), BR (28), IN (23), DE (22), AU (21), IT (16), TH (13), ES (9), MX (8), TW (7) and IL (7); 349 records carry no country. By region, Europe accounts for roughly 191 victims, APAC 96, Latin America and the Caribbean 59, and Canada 30. Structurally the sector shows three distinct victim populations that behave very differently: US K-12 districts (overwhelmingly the largest count, typically small IT teams, frequently posted by Interlock, Qilin, Medusa and INC Ransom), universities and research institutions (higher data value, research IP and often regulated health data, targeted by Qilin, Rhysida and Fog), and edtech/SIS/LMS vendors, which are numerically rare but produce catastrophic aggregation events - the PowerSchool SIS compromise (Dec 2024) and the Instructure/Canvas LMS breaches (May 2026) each affected thousands of institutions from a single intrusion. Extortion economics in the leak-site data are modest relative to other sectors: only 12 of 1,296 records carried an explicit ransom figure, clustered between $50,000 and $400,000 (largely Medusa postings against US K-12 districts), with the notable outlier being Asia University, Taiwan (crazyhunter, March 2025) at $1,500,000. Only 21 records disclosed a data volume, ranging from 20MB to 1.5TB. Press coverage is attached to just 170 of 1,296 records (13%), meaning the large majority of education ransomware events receive no public reporting, and loss figures for the sector must be inferred from survey data rather than incident disclosure.
data_sources_used: ransomware.live API v2 - /v2/sectorvictims/Education (1,296 victim records, retrieved 20 July 2026)
ransomwatch (joshhighet/ransomwatch) posts.json via raw.githubusercontent.com - 16,072 leak-site posts, 507 education-matching
Sophos - The State of Ransomware in Education 2025
Comparitech - Education Ransomware Roundup 2025 and US schools/colleges ransomware cost study
IBM - Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025
Verizon - Data Breach Investigations Report (2025 and 2026 editions)
Coveware by Veeam - quarterly ransomware reports 2025

Press reporting: BleepingComputer, The Record, TechCrunch, EdWeek, The 74, SecurityWeek, Infosecurity Magazine, Inside Higher Ed, The Hacker News, HIPAA Journal, Cybersecurity Dive, K-12 Dive, Campus Technology, WBAL-TV, Wikipedia (British Library cyberattack; 2026 Canvas security incident)
data_source_notes: STEP 1 (base data): The documented path https://api.ransomware.live/v2/victims/sector/Education does NOT exist - it returns HTTP 200 with the API's HTML documentation landing page rather than JSON, and WebFetch on it followed a 302 to www.ransomware.live/api. Endpoint discovery against /v2/sectors confirmed the correct route is /v2/sectorvictims/{sector}; https://api.ransomware.live/v2/sectorvictims/Education returned 1.27MB of valid JSON with 1,296 records. Sibling reports built against the documented path should be re-checked. Retrieval was also constrained by the documented 1-request-per-minute-per-endpoint limit: the first attempt returned {"message": "1 per 1 minute"}, and the fetch succeeded on retry after a 65-second wait, per the stated retry guidance. Two tooling issues were worked around and are worth recording: (a) curl in this environment failed with error 43 on every invocation, so all HTTP retrieval was done via PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest; (b) Windows PowerShell 5.1's ConvertFrom-Json is case-insensitive on object keys and aborted on the nested 'infostealer.infostealer_stats' object, which contains both 'RedLine' and 'Redline' - all parsing and aggregation was therefore done in Python 3.12. Returned fields were: activity, attackdate, claim_url, country, data_size, description, discovered, domain, group, infostealer, press, ransom, screenshot, url, victim. Field completeness is poor for loss modelling: press present on 170/1,296 (13%), an explicit ransom figure on 12/1,296 (0.9%), data_size on 21/1,296 (1.6%), and country absent on 349/1,296 (27%). Several victim names carry mojibake from upstream encoding (e.g. 'University of G?vle', 'Universidad Nacional Aut?noma de M?xico'). Note also that 'activity' is the leak-site operator's own sector tag, so some tagged victims are libraries, museums, unions and training bodies rather than schools (e.g. Phoenix Art Museum, Pennsylvania State Education Association, labiennale.org), and conversely major education events do not appear at all when the actor never posted a leak page - PowerSchool, the single largest education incident in the dataset's period, is absent for exactly this reason. Leak-site counts are claims, not confirmations, and undercount both non-posting actors and victims who paid pre-publication. STEP 2 (supplementation): mixed results. https://www.ransomlook.io/api/search?query=university FAILED - HTTP 400 via WebFetch; GET https://www.ransomlook.io/api/search/university returned 404, https://www.ransomlook.io/api/sectors returned 404, and POST to /api/search returned 405 Method Not Allowed, so the RansomLook search API appears retired or restructured and no data was obtained from it. https://ransomwhat.telemetry.ltd/posts.json FAILED at the given URL - it 302-redirects to ransomwatch.telemetry.ltd and serves an HTML landing page, not JSON. This was recovered by falling back to the project's canonical data file at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/joshhighet/ransomwatch/main/posts.json, which returned 16,072 posts (fields: post_title, group_name, discovered). Keyword filtering for education terms yielded 507 education-matching posts by year - 2021 (57), 2022 (105), 2023 (193), 2024 (112), 2025 (40) - with top groups lockbit3 (58), vicesociety (50), pysa (39), rhysida (39), FOG (27), clop (22), incransom (21), alphv (18). This independently corroborates the ransomware.live group ranking and the 2023 peak, but the dataset is STALE: its most recent post is dated 16 June 2025, so its 2025 figure is a partial year and it provides no 2026 coverage. It was used only as corroboration, never as a primary count. STEP 3 (incident enrichment): all incident details below were sourced from named press reporting via WebSearch and WebFetch, not from the leak-site description fields, which are attacker-authored marketing copy and in several cases explicitly AI-generated by ransomware.live ('[AI generated]' prefix). Attacker claims are labelled as claims throughout. Where a figure is not in public reporting it is written as 'not publicly disclosed' rather than estimated. STEP 5 (aggregate stats): Sophos is the primary source because it is the only major study that reports Lower Education and Higher Education as separate strata. One conflict is flagged: Comparitech's US schools/colleges cost study returned $2.54bn in estimated damages for 2018 to mid-2024 when fetched directly, while search result titles for the same page cite $9.45bn, indicating the page has been revised across differing scopes; the disputed cumulative-damages total is therefore omitted and only the stable per-incident downtime figures from that study are cited.

hazard_categories.category: Initial Access via Open and Federated Campus Environments
hazard_categories.description: Education networks are architecturally adversarial to containment. Universities operate deliberately open networks supporting public research collaboration, guest access, self-managed student devices and thousands of transient accounts per year, while K-12 districts run flat networks with minimal segmentation and small IT teams. Sophos found exploited vulnerabilities to be the single largest root cause in higher education (35% of attacks) and phishing the leading cause in lower education (22%), reflecting the two different failure modes. Verizon DBIR data has repeatedly placed social engineering and system intrusion as the dominant education breach patterns.
subcategories: Unpatched internet-facing infrastructure (VPN concentrators, VMware ESXi, Citrix, file transfer appliances)
Phishing and business email compromise against faculty, staff and payroll
Compromised credentials and absent or partial MFA on student/staff SSO
Federated identity and SSO trust chains (Shibboleth, InCommon, eduGAIN, Entra ID) enabling lateral movement across institutions
BYOD and unmanaged student-owned devices on production VLANs
Flat, unsegmented K-12 district networks linking administrative and instructional systems
Research collaboration links, shared HPC clusters and inter-institutional data sharing
Remote and hybrid learning infrastructure, exposed RDP and legacy remote access
Seasonal staffing churn, adjunct and contractor accounts, and stale account deprovisioning

hazard_categories.category: Extortion Leverage from Minors' and Student Data
hazard_categories.description: Education is uniquely coercible because the hostage data belongs largely to children. Actors have moved from encryption-first to exfiltration-led extortion and apply pressure through channels unavailable in other sectors: publishing psychological evaluations, special-education records and abuse reports, and contacting students and parents directly. In the LAUSD and Minneapolis cases the leaked corpora included student psychological assessments, and in Minneapolis campus security blueprints - creating physical-safety as well as privacy harm. Sophos recorded extortion-only (no encryption) attacks rising in both education strata.
subcategories: Publication of minors' PII, disciplinary, special-education and counselling records
Release of student psychological and medical assessments
Direct contact with parents, students and staff to amplify pressure (triple extortion)
Leak of campus security blueprints, floor plans and access-control layouts
FERPA/COPPA notification exposure used as negotiating leverage
Reputational leverage over admissions, enrolment and donor confidence
Timing of attacks to term start, exams, enrolment or financial-aid deadlines
Re-extortion of individual institutions after a vendor has already paid
Auction and resale of student datasets on leak sites

hazard_categories.category: Third-Party and Edtech Vendor Concentration Risk
hazard_categories.description: The single most severe systemic hazard in the sector. A handful of SIS, LMS and assessment platforms serve most of the addressable market, so one vendor intrusion becomes a correlated loss across thousands of insureds simultaneously. PowerSchool (Dec 2024) reached a claimed 62.4 million students and 9.5 million teachers across approximately 6,505 districts from one compromised credential; Instructure/Canvas (May 2026) was claimed to affect 275 million users across roughly 9,000 institutions. Verizon's 2026 DBIR reported third-party involvement in 48% of breaches with supply-chain breaches up 60%. For a cyber-insurance portfolio this is the dominant aggregation exposure in the education book.
subcategories: Student information system (SIS) platform compromise
Learning management system (LMS) platform compromise
Single-vendor concentration across a large book of district/university insureds
Downstream re-extortion of individual schools using vendor-stolen data
Managed service providers and regional education service agencies serving many districts
Tuition, bursar and payment processor compromise
Assessment, proctoring, transcript and admissions platforms
Cloud file transfer and third-party SaaS (e.g. mass MOVEit/Cleo-style exploitation reaching education via clop)
Contractual gaps in vendor breach notification, indemnity and data-deletion assurance

hazard_categories.description: Education is the rare sector in which a substantial share of the resident population is both technically capable and directly motivated to attack the institution's systems - for grade alteration, exam access or reputational reasons - while holding legitimate network credentials. The PowerSchool intrusion was ultimately attributed by the US DOJ to a 19-year-old university student, who pleaded guilty. Insider events blur the ransomware/fraud boundary and complicate coverage triggers.
subcategories: Student credential abuse and grade or transcript alteration
Attacks originating from enrolled students against their own institution
Faculty and staff insider data theft
Credential sharing, shadow IT and unauthorised SaaS in departments
Initial access broker purchase of student/staff credentials from infostealer logs
Departing staff and contractor access retention
Negligent insiders and misconfigured shares exposing student records

hazard_categories.description: Education carries a dense, overlapping and unusually child-focused compliance regime, so a single ransomware event generates parallel regulatory tracks. FERPA and COPPA apply federally in the US, layered with state student-privacy statutes and state breach laws; UK and EU institutions face UK GDPR/GDPR and ICO scrutiny; universities holding clinical or research-health data additionally trigger HIPAA. Notification is frequently slow - Minneapolis took seven months to notify 105,617 people, and the University of Hawai'i Cancer Center's delay in notifying study participants drew specific criticism - which compounds regulatory and class-action risk.
subcategories: FERPA (US student education records)
COPPA and state student-privacy laws (e.g. SOPIPA-style statutes)
State breach-notification statutes and attorney-general inquiries
UK GDPR / EU GDPR and ICO or DPA enforcement
HIPAA exposure for university medical centres, clinics and health research
Research funder, IRB and human-subjects data obligations
Class-action litigation on behalf of students, parents and staff
Delayed-notification liability and credit-monitoring remediation costs
Public-records and transparency obligations for public institutions

hazard_categories.category: Operational Disruption of Instruction and Institutional Continuity
hazard_categories.description: Unlike most commercial insureds, schools cannot fail over to a degraded manual mode: an encrypted district frequently closes entirely. Highline Public Schools shut all 34 schools for three days; the British Library's core services were disrupted for months. Comparitech measured an average of 10.7 days of downtime per education incident, peaking at 12.6 days in 2023. Lost instructional days carry statutory make-up obligations, transport and meal-programme knock-ons, and in higher education can delay terms, research grants and graduation.
subcategories: Full school or campus closure and lost instructional days
Statutory make-up day and calendar-extension obligations
Loss of attendance, gradebook, timetabling and transport systems
Disruption to free/reduced meal programmes and student services
Payroll, HR and accounts-payable outage
Research interruption, lost experiments and grant milestone failure
Admissions, enrolment, registration and financial-aid disruption
Extended rebuild and device re-imaging across large fleets
Library, catalogue and digital collection outage

hazard_categories.category: Underfunded Security Posture and Recovery Capability
hazard_categories.description: The sector's loss severity is driven less by attacker sophistication than by chronic under-resourcing. Sophos found lack of expertise and limited incident-response capacity cited by 42% each in lower education, and 49% of higher education institutions citing unknown security gaps. Backup reliability has degraded: recovery from backups fell to 59% in lower education and 47% in higher education. Public institutions face procurement cycles, capital-budget constraints and elected-board approval that slow both hardening and response.
subcategories: Small or single-person IT teams in K-12 districts
Legacy and end-of-life systems retained on constrained capital budgets
Backup compromise, untested restores and insufficient offline copies
Absence of 24/7 monitoring, EDR coverage gaps and alert fatigue
Limited or absent cyber insurance and incident-response retainers
Slow public procurement and board-approval cycles
Reserve depletion funding recovery (British Library used c.40% of reserves)
IT staff burnout and turnover following incidents
Decentralised university IT with no central authority over departmental systems

exposure_categories.category: Student Information Systems (SIS) and Core Records
exposure_categories.description: The system of record for enrolment, demographics, attendance, discipline and transcripts, and the highest-value single target in education because it concentrates minors' PII for an entire district or institution in one platform. SIS compromise is both a direct exposure at the institution and, via the vendor, the sector's principal aggregation event - the PowerSchool intrusion reached a claimed 62.4 million students and 9.5 million teachers across approximately 6,505 districts.
subcategories: Enrolment, demographic and household records
Attendance and truancy data
Disciplinary and behavioural records
Transcripts, grades and academic history
Special-education (IEP/504) records
Immunisation and student health records held in SIS
Emergency contact and guardian/custody information
Free and reduced-price meal eligibility (income-linked)
Vendor-hosted SIS instances and SIS data warehouses

exposure_categories.category: Learning Management Systems, Gradebooks and Instructional Platforms
exposure_categories.description: The day-to-day instructional layer - LMS, gradebook, courseware, assessment and proctoring tools. Outage halts teaching directly, and the platforms hold years of coursework, private messaging and behavioural data. The May 2026 Instructure/Canvas incident demonstrated the scale: attackers claimed 3.6TB covering 275 million users across roughly 9,000 institutions, including private student-teacher messages, in a platform used by 41% of US higher education institutions.
subcategories: LMS platforms (Canvas, Blackboard, Moodle, Schoology, Google Classroom)
Gradebooks and assignment/submission repositories
Private messaging between students, teachers and staff
Online assessment, exam and remote-proctoring systems
Lecture capture, courseware and digital content libraries
Plagiarism detection and academic-integrity tooling
Course rosters, section data and LTI integrations
Single sign-on tokens and API keys linking LMS to institutional identity

exposure_categories.category: Financial Aid, Bursar, Payroll and Payment Systems
exposure_categories.description: Education institutions process tuition, financial aid, donations, payroll and vendor payments, and financial-aid files in particular concentrate exactly the identity elements needed for fraud - SSNs, bank details and full household income data (FAFSA). Encryption here halts payroll and disbursement; exfiltration produces the sector's highest per-record identity-theft severity.
subcategories: Financial aid, FAFSA, scholarship and loan records
Bursar, tuition billing and student account systems
Payroll, HR and benefits data for staff and faculty
Bank account and direct deposit details
Social Security numbers and taxpayer identifiers
Third-party tuition payment processors and gateways
Procurement, accounts payable and vendor master files
Campus card and stored-value/dining account systems
Grant accounting and research funding administration

exposure_categories.category: Research Data, Intellectual Property and Regulated Research Health Data
exposure_categories.description: The exposure unique to higher education. Universities hold pre-publication research, proprietary and licensed datasets, export-controlled work and long-running human-subjects cohorts. The University of Manchester attack reached NHS records for 1.1 million patients gathered from over 200 hospitals for medical research, and the University of Hawai'i Cancer Center incident exposed decades-old epidemiological cohort data affecting up to 1.15 million individuals - demonstrating that research archives create liability for populations who were never students or staff.
subcategories: Human-subjects research cohorts and longitudinal study data
Clinical, patient and genomic research datasets (HIPAA-regulated)
Pre-publication research, grant applications and unpublished results
Patents, licensing pipelines and technology-transfer records
Export-controlled, defence and dual-use research
Industry-sponsored and contract research under NDA
HPC clusters, lab instrumentation and research computing storage
Licensed third-party datasets with contractual breach penalties
IRB records and participant consent/identity linkage files

exposure_categories.category: Minors' PII and Sensitive Student Welfare Records
exposure_categories.description: The sector's most reputationally and legally explosive exposure. Beyond routine PII, schools hold counselling notes, psychological evaluations, abuse and safeguarding reports, and custody arrangements for children who cannot consent and whose identities remain exploitable for decades. Both LAUSD and Minneapolis saw student psychological assessments published after refusing to pay, and Baltimore City Public Schools' 2025 incident exposed SSNs and driver's licence data for thousands of students and staff.
subcategories: Minors' names, dates of birth, addresses and SSNs
Counselling, mental-health and psychological assessment records
Child protection, safeguarding and abuse reports
Custody, foster-care and guardianship arrangements
Juvenile justice and prior-conviction referral records
Health, disability and medication records
Immigration status and English-learner designations
Photographs, biometrics and student ID imagery
Long-tail identity-theft exposure (dormant credit files of minors)

exposure_categories.category: Campus Operational Technology and Physical Safety Systems
exposure_categories.description: Schools and campuses run building and safety infrastructure on the same networks as administrative IT, so ransomware translates directly into physical-safety consequences and closure decisions. The Minneapolis breach was confirmed by analysts to have exposed school security blueprints - a worst-case outcome in which stolen data creates ongoing physical risk to children that no notification or credit monitoring can remediate.
subcategories: Door access control, badging and electronic locking systems
CCTV, video surveillance and monitoring platforms
Fire alarm, intrusion detection and emergency notification systems
HVAC, boiler and building management systems
Dormitory and residence-hall access and utilities
Bus routing, fleet telematics and student transport tracking
Bell schedules, PA systems and lockdown/emergency controls
Campus security floor plans, blueprints and camera placement maps
Laboratory, athletic facility and dining OT systems

exposure_categories.description: University advancement systems hold high-net-worth individuals' financial profiles, giving histories, wealth-screening assessments and private correspondence. This data is disproportionately valuable relative to its volume, and its exposure damages the institution's fundraising capacity - a material revenue line for higher education - well beyond the incident itself. The University of Manchester breach included alumni records alongside current student data.
subcategories: Alumni contact, employment and biographical records
Donor giving histories and pledge commitments
Wealth screening and capacity/propensity ratings
Major-gift prospect research and confidential correspondence
Payment instruments and recurring donation details
Endowment, trust and planned-giving records
Board, trustee and named-benefactor information
Event, membership and affinity programme data

exposure_categories.category: Third-Party Edtech, Cloud and Identity Infrastructure
exposure_categories.description: Modern institutions outsource most of their data estate, so a large share of exposure sits outside the insured's own perimeter and outside its control. This is the exposure that converts individual education risks into portfolio-level correlated loss, and Verizon's 2026 DBIR reported third parties featuring in 48% of breaches with supply-chain breaches up 60% year over year.
subcategories: SIS, LMS and assessment vendors (aggregation nodes)
Managed service providers and regional education service agencies
Cloud tenancies (Microsoft 365, Google Workspace) and OAuth token estates
Federated identity providers and SSO trust fabric (Shibboleth, InCommon, eduGAIN)
Managed file transfer and data exchange platforms
Payment processors, tuition plans and collections agencies
Library systems, catalogues, e-resource and publisher platforms
Transcript, credentialing, admissions and enrolment-verification services
Backup, DR and archival providers
Student wellbeing, tutoring, safety-monitoring and communications apps

example_incidents.victim: PowerSchool (SIS vendor serving K-12 districts in the US, Canada and elsewhere)
example_incidents.group: Not a named ransomware brand - single-actor extortion; US DOJ charged Matthew D. Lane, then a 19-year-old student at Assumption University
example_incidents.summary: The defining edtech aggregation event. An attacker used compromised credentials to access PowerSchool's PowerSource support portal and exfiltrate student and teacher data from the hosted SIS environment. PowerSchool paid an extortion demand in exchange for a video purporting to show deletion of the only copy of the data. The deletion proved worthless: in May 2025 the same data was used to extort individual school districts directly in Canada and North Carolina, with attackers sending samples to schools. PowerSchool stated it did not believe this was a new intrusion because the samples matched the December theft. This is the clearest available demonstration that paying for a deletion promise transfers no risk downstream, and that a single vendor compromise generates thousands of correlated district-level losses.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Total programme cost not publicly disclosed. PowerSchool offered two years of identity protection and credit monitoring to affected students and educators; class-action litigation followed. Individual district remediation and notification costs were not publicly itemised.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Approximately $2.85 million in bitcoin demanded and PAID by PowerSchool, per US Department of Justice court documents made public 20 May 2025. Amounts sought in the subsequent district-level extortion attempts were not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: No mass encryption event - this was exfiltration-only extortion, so districts did not suffer the closure pattern typical of encryption attacks. Recovery centred on notification, credit monitoring, credential resets and multi-jurisdiction regulatory response, extending well beyond a year and reopening when re-extortion began in May 2025.
example_incidents.data_impact: The attacker claimed data on 62.4 million students and 9.5 million teachers across approximately 6,505 school districts in the US, Canada and other countries. Exposed fields included names, addresses, dates of birth, contact details, and for some individuals Social Security numbers and medical/grade information. Affected populations are overwhelmingly minors, whose identity exposure persists for decades.

example_incidents.date: 2026-05-01 (intrusion 29-30 April 2026; second breach within roughly two weeks)
example_incidents.summary: Described in reporting as the largest education-sector breach on record. ShinyHunters exploited Instructure's Free-For-Teacher (FFT) programme - which allowed educators to create Canvas accounts without institutional verification - to reach production data, then breached the platform a second time within about two weeks. After Instructure missed the initial 7 May negotiation deadline, the group escalated by defacing Canvas login portals at roughly 330 institutions and pivoting to direct school-by-school extortion with a final 12 May deadline. Instructure reached a payment agreement on 11 May, one day before the leak deadline. The incident is the purest example of LMS vendor concentration risk: Canvas is used by 41% of US higher education institutions, so a single platform intrusion simultaneously exposed thousands of otherwise unconnected insureds.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed. Institutional costs spanned incident response, forensic review, portal remediation after defacement, and notification across thousands of schools.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Ransom PAID by Instructure under an agreement reached 11 May 2026; the amount was not publicly disclosed. Attackers reportedly returned the data and supplied 'shred logs' as claimed proof of destruction - the same unverifiable deletion assurance seen in the PowerSchool case.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Instructure took Canvas, Canvas Beta and Canvas Test offline on 7 May 2026 for investigation and restored service the following day; Canvas Data 2 and Canvas Beta had been in maintenance since 1 May. The Free-For-Teacher account programme was permanently shut down as a remediation measure. Roughly 330 institutions additionally had to remediate defaced login portals.
example_incidents.data_impact: ShinyHunters claimed 3.6TB covering 275 million users across approximately 9,000 institutions (reporting also cites 8,809 universities, education ministries and other bodies) - figures Instructure has not confirmed. Instructure confirmed exposure of names, email addresses, student ID numbers and some private messages between Canvas users, and stated there was no evidence that passwords, financial data or SSNs were taken. Attacker leak-site copy claimed billions of private student-teacher and student-student messages.

example_incidents.group: noescape (per ransomware.live leak-site attribution; press reporting did not definitively confirm the group)
example_incidents.summary: A university research-archive breach that illustrates how higher education accumulates liability for populations who were never students or staff. Attackers reached data from the Multiethnic Cohort (MEC) Study, a longitudinal epidemiological study established in 1993, plus files from three other diet-and-cancer studies. Compounding the event, the university did not notify affected study participants for roughly four months - a delay that drew specific public criticism and independent regulatory risk. Notably, the university PAID to prevent publication, making this one of the few education cases with a confirmed payment decision.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed. Costs included ransom payment, third-party forensic and recovery support, and notification plus remediation for up to 1.15 million individuals.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Ransom PAID - the centre worked with third-party cybersecurity experts to obtain a decryption tool and paid to prevent publication of the stolen data. The amount was not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Encrypted data was recovered using a decryption tool obtained through the payment. Specific outage duration was not publicly disclosed. Notification lagged roughly four months behind discovery, with the centre compiling names and addresses for study participants well after the August 2025 intrusion.
example_incidents.data_impact: Up to 1.15 million individuals affected (some reporting cites approximately 1.2 million). Exposed data included Social Security numbers and driver's licence numbers sourced from the Hawai'i State Department of Transportation, and City and County of Honolulu voter registration records from 1998. Much of the affected population were research study participants rather than students or employees.

example_incidents.group: Not publicly attributed (district confirmed ransomware; FBI engaged)
example_incidents.summary: The canonical K-12 operational-disruption case. Highline, a Washington state district of 34 schools serving roughly 17,500 students and 2,000 staff, detected the intrusion on a Saturday and immediately isolated critical systems - then closed every school and all activities for three days because core instructional and safety systems could not be trusted. It demonstrates the sector's defining characteristic for insurers: a school district has no degraded operating mode, so business interruption manifests as total closure of an essential public service, with statutory make-up obligations and knock-on effects to transport and meal programmes.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed. Costs included district-wide re-imaging of all student and staff devices, third-party forensic engagement, and three days of lost instruction across 34 schools.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not publicly disclosed - the district declined to say how much was demanded, citing the ongoing investigation, and did not publicly confirm any payment.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: All schools and activities closed for three days, from Monday 9 September through Wednesday 11 September 2024, reopening Thursday 12 September. Network systems remained disrupted into October 2024, when all student and staff devices had been re-imaged - roughly a month of degraded operation after classes resumed.
example_incidents.data_impact: The district confirmed that highly sensitive personal, financial and medical data was breached. The precise number of affected students and staff was not publicly disclosed in the reporting reviewed.

example_incidents.summary: The UK's national library, described as one of the worst cyber incidents in British history. Rhysida rendered almost all VMware ESXi servers unavailable, taking down the website, on-site services and Wi-Fi; the library remained physically open but could accept only cash payments. The institution refused to pay and Rhysida published the stolen material. The case is the reference point for catastrophic recovery severity in a public, non-commercial education/research body: the recovery cost dwarfed the ransom demand by an order of magnitude, and the library had to consume roughly 40% of its financial reserves - a funding mechanism with no analogue in the commercial sector and a key consideration for public-institution insureds.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Approximately GBP 6-7 million in recovery costs, funded from roughly 40% of the library's financial reserves - about ten times the ransom demanded.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: 20 bitcoin demanded, approximately GBP 596,000 at the time. NOT PAID - the library refused, and Rhysida published the data.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Services were severely disrupted for months. The main catalogue returned online on 15 January 2024 in read-only format, roughly two and a half months after the attack, with other services expected to remain unavailable for months beyond that. Recovery was complicated by legacy infrastructure and constrained funding, documented in the library's own transparency reporting and subsequent academic analysis.
example_incidents.data_impact: Approximately 600GB of material leaked publicly after refusal to pay, including internal documents and staff and user data. Full affected-individual counts were not publicly itemised in the reporting reviewed.

example_incidents.group: Not publicly attributed to a named leak-site brand; triple-extortion tactics consistent with groups active against UK/US higher education in 2023
example_incidents.date: 2023-06-05 (intrusion began 5 June 2023; detected 9 June; containment from 14 June)
example_incidents.summary: The clearest illustration of research-data liability in higher education. Attackers reached a research archive holding NHS patient records gathered from more than 200 hospitals for medical research purposes - including major-trauma patient reports and treatment records for victims of terrorist attacks - alongside current student and alumni data. Attackers then emailed students and staff directly threatening to sell their data, a triple-extortion pressure tactic. The incident triggered questions in UK health and education policy about universities holding national-scale clinical datasets under research governance rather than clinical security controls.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Not publicly disclosed. No public confirmation of payment; the university worked with the ICO, NCSC and National Crime Agency.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Detected 9 June 2023 with containment beginning 14 June. Specific outage duration and full recovery timeline were not publicly disclosed; response ran in parallel with ICO and NCSC engagement.
example_incidents.data_impact: Around 250GB of data accessed. Included NHS records relating to 1.1 million patients across more than 200 hospitals, gathered for medical research - with NHS numbers and the first three letters of patients' postcodes among the fields, plus major-trauma and terrorist-attack victim treatment data. Separately, student and alumni data was leaked including names, contact details, gender, dates of birth, university ID numbers and fee status. Students and staff received direct threats to sell their data.

example_incidents.victim: Minneapolis Public Schools (Special School District No. 1)
example_incidents.summary: The reference case for extortion harm to minors and for notification failure. Medusa demanded $1 million with a 17 March deadline, posted the district on its leak site with a countdown, offered to sell the data to any buyer for $1 million, and offered the district the option to pay $50,000 per additional day of delay. The district refused and restored from internal backups - but Medusa then published the files. Analysts confirmed the leaked corpus included school security blueprints, a physical-safety exposure that cannot be remediated by notification or credit monitoring. The district publicly characterised the event as an 'encryption event' and did not notify the 105,617 affected individuals until September 2023, seven months later.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed. Costs included forensic investigation, restoration from backups, and notification plus credit monitoring for 105,617 individuals.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: $1,000,000 demanded by Medusa with a 17 March 2023 deadline; the leak site also offered a $50,000-per-day deadline extension and listed the data for outright purchase at $1 million. NOT PAID - the district restored from internal backups and Medusa published the stolen files.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: Widespread digital disruption following the 17 February 2023 encryption event; the district recovered encrypted data from internal backups rather than paying. Precise system-restoration duration was not publicly disclosed. Notification took seven months, completing in September 2023.
example_incidents.data_impact: 105,617 people notified as affected. Nearly 200,000 individual files containing sensitive student and educator information were released publicly, including student psychological and welfare records. Cybersecurity experts confirmed campus security maps and school security blueprints were among the leaked material - creating ongoing physical-safety risk to students.

example_incidents.date: 2022-09-03 (attack 3 September 2022; leak-site posting 30 September 2022; data published 2 October 2022)
example_incidents.summary: The attack that made K-12 ransomware a national policy issue in the US. Vice Society - the group that dominated education targeting in this period, ranking fourth all-time in the Education dataset with 63 victims - dwelled in the network of the second-largest US school district for over a month, from 31 July to 3 September 2022. LAUSD publicly refused to pay on the principle that 'dollars must be used to fund students and education' and that paying never guarantees full recovery, following FBI guidance. Vice Society published the full 500GB trove in retaliation. The leaked data's contents - student psychological assessments, health and COVID-19 test data, and prior conviction reports - established the template for how education extortion inflicts harm on minors specifically.
example_incidents.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed as a single figure. The district funded incident response, credit monitoring for affected individuals including contractors whose SSNs were exposed, and a subsequent security programme uplift.
example_incidents.ransom_demanded_or_paid: Demand amount not publicly disclosed. NOT PAID - LAUSD publicly refused, stating public dollars are better spent on students than on criminals, and Vice Society published the data on its leak blog on 2 October 2022.
example_incidents.downtime_and_recovery: The attack disrupted district systems in early September 2022 at the start of the school year, though schools remained open. Threat actors had persistent access from 31 July to 3 September 2022 before detection - a dwell time of over a month. Full remediation timeline was not publicly disclosed.
example_incidents.data_impact: 500GB of data stolen and published. The trove included student psychological assessments, health information including COVID-19 test data, and prior conviction reports. LAUSD separately confirmed that contractors' Social Security numbers were among the stolen data. Passport data and other sensitive identifiers were also reported as potentially included.
